All the countless transformations and growth of plants and animals between Heaven and Earth cannot be reckoned in their thousands and hundreds. Their forms are strange and varied, great and small intermingled, as vast and boundless as a misty sea. It allows one to see everything clearly at a glance, leaving nothing hidden — this is precisely why such illustrations cannot be dispensed with. Therefore, those in the world who have spoken of materia medica, from Li Ji of the Tang and Su Song of the Song onward, have never failed to value such illustrated collections. By the time Li Shizhen of the Ming compiled his Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), it magnificently gathered together the great achievements of all the various schools, and scholars since have taken it as their standard reference. However...

...its illustrations are in fact not worth looking at — why is this? I once obtained an original printing of the Gangmu and examined it. As for the fine and minute goods brought by trading ships from distant lands beyond the sea, they are all laid out before us, obtainable without even leaving one's desk—the diligence behind this may truly be called great. Now birds and beasts are things that mutually serve human use, yet the old classifications of livestock established in ancient times were not sufficient to elaborate fully on this subject; those who look into it cannot help but feel this as a regret.

This compilation by Kan'en, built upon the detailed structure of the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica), has further gathered extensive research, making things as clear as if one were watching a fire, illuminating what was previously obscure and profound, so as to benefit students who come after. To call him a worthy successor and meritorious heir to Master Li (Li Shizhen)—who could possibly object to such a description?

Though I myself am not especially clever, I too have long taken an interest in this field of study. Having known Kan'en for a long time, I could not refuse his request, and so I have written this preface for him.

Preface to the Honzō Zufu

Among the things people love, none is loved more than life; among the things people hate, none is hated more than death. If one wishes to leave people without regret amid the crises of illness and the boundary between life and death, what other recourse is there but medicine? The Way of medicine is but one, yet its responsibility is extremely heavy and pressing. And in the course of administering treatment, nothing can be accomplished without reliance upon medicinal substances. The relationship between medicine and its materia medica is as urgent and indispensable as that between a general and his soldiers. Even if one has an excellent general or a miraculous physician, if he is left to stand with folded arms, he can only wait helplessly for the patient's decline and death.

...only this. Therefore victory or defeat in battle depends on the quality of provisions, whether strong or weak, suitable or not; and whether medicines are of fine or coarse quality is likewise something one cannot but be careful about.

This is precisely why the study of medicinal herbs (honzōgaku) cannot be treated as anything but urgent and important. Since the sages of high antiquity first compiled its classics, every age has had those who recorded and transmitted it, until in the Ming dynasty Li Shizhen compiled and arranged it, bringing it to great completion. Yet although he searched thoroughly and composed his explanations, in gathering and preserving material his accounts were sometimes careless or mistaken, not a few; and at times he focused solely on flavor and energy (qi) while leaving gaps and omissions.

As for form and appearance — if one now tests this against the climates of East and West, large and small, thick and thin, good and bad already differ one from another; and if one does not truly know what a given thing is, shallow people will guess at it rashly and use it accordingly — there are such cases. Those who suffer harm from careless, unexamined application of it also exist. As for scholarship on this matter, failing to get its principles right is no small or trivial matter.

Then there appeared masters such as Wakamizu (若水稲先生), after whom this field of study became considerably clarified; and Kaibara, Matsuoka, Abe, Tamura, Ota, Ono and other teachers carried it further and made it flourish one after another. As a result, its theories became ever more refined and precise — though the pace of this advancement has been at times urgent, at times slow.

[The text] handed down [uses] written characters, yet how can one truly capture the image of a thing through words alone? To truly know an object, it must be like the time when Yu cast his bronze cauldrons so that people could recognize and avoid demons and monsters—only after seeing the actual form could they know it.

This is why mere words are insufficient to convey the essence—they cannot fully express the nature, temperament, and flavor of a thing the way that an image depicting its visible form can. Because the visible shape of a thing is best shown through pictures, this is the very reason why I have compiled this illustrated herbal.

Flowers and fruits, if not accurately rendered, may be mistaken for cats, and students who come after may fall into doubt and confusion as a result.

Illustrations may sometimes be imperfect and clumsy in execution, yet still convey some impression.

Honzo Zufu
Volume 50
Page 3

If one does not see something with one's own eyes, understanding remains unclear. Yet the world contains so many things, scattered across east and west, far and near, blooming and withering at different times, amid mountains and seas full of danger—how could one possibly see them all firsthand?

Thus images and words must work together—it cannot be otherwise. Of these three means [direct observation, verbal description, and illustration], each has its own particular day of use.

One cannot possibly provide illustrations for every single object in existence—there are always gaps. Verbal description also has its limits.

There is always one more layer removed in explanation; even if a description is extremely detailed, when one reads it, there remains a need to form a mental image from the words before true understanding is achieved, and even then doubts and confusions may linger.

But with illustrations, it is not so—one glance makes everything perfectly clear, with no need for further labor of the mind.

translation:
Ever since my youth I have been fond of learning, always taking up the books of many scholars and reading them closely. Examining these matters, I probed deeply and, weighing the various theories, assigned each plant to its proper type—its seedlings, leaves, flowers, and fruit—sketching them from life according to the season, so that none of their peculiarities were missed.

I searched the mountains and wilds, transplanting specimens into garden plots and pots, in all more than two thousand kinds. Even from remote and out-of-the-way places, wherever my eyes beheld a plant I drew it without exception. In this way, over more than twenty years, I gradually completed a number of volumes, which I have titled "Honzō Bigafu" (Illustrated Compendium of Medicinal Plants). In making these illustrations I exhausted my skill to the utmost, applying color with the greatest care and devoting all my spirit to the work.

[As for the purpose of this work] — by consulting it even a child could, within a single glance, without wasting words or expense, distinguish what a certain object truly is. It would spare physicians of the world the trouble of hastily guessing at remedies, for by using it in their practice they could rely on it with confidence, judging that the name and substance of a plant are better established by careful comparison than left to guesswork. If it can be rightly applied to the treatment of illness, then perhaps the people of the whole realm — in matters of life, death, and fate — might be spared regret. In the critical moments between life and death, may this work preserve [something of value] for the world to come.

Ezo-udo

In Edo, the udo found in the mountains around Zōjōji Temple

Shōma (Cimicifuga / Bugbane) — reading: kōma
Also called: Kibute
[Found in:] Hizen Province
Higo Province

It grows in Toshima District of Musashi Province, in Noshū, on Mount Nikkō, and in various other provinces. The leaves have three branches bearing nine leaflets, resembling the leaves of Udo (Aralia), hard and glossy with serrated edges. The stem reaches three to four feet in height, with a flower spike appearing at its tip; the small flowers are shaped like heron feathers and are white in color. One variety has a black root, with bluish-white flesh and a bitter taste.

One type: the large-leaved kind.

Commonly called "Oni-tsura Shōma" (Demon-face Shōma), it has three leaves on a single stem, resembling the Kaidō (Chinese flowering crabapple) but larger — a single leaf being exceptionally large, which is why it is likened to a demon's face. The stem emerges from the middle of the leaf.

Mountain Jigo (Amana)
Reading: Amafu

This plant grows at Dōkanyama in Musashi Province, and is also found in other provinces. In the third month it sends up shoots. Jasminum (matsuri / mogiri)

This Ryukyuan sandalwood-like plant was brought to Edo during the Bunsei era. It is a small tree with thin, vine-like branches. Its leaves resemble those of the winter jasmine (keishunka), growing oppositely in sets of five leaflets. In summer, five-petaled white flowers bloom from between the stems, shaped somewhat like the "hōshika" flower but smaller, and fragrant. It does not bear fruit separately; its seeds resemble bamboo rice and are blackish-green in color.

[Label:] Jasminum odoratum
Natsushiki-yumu (Latin name)

Honzō Zufu
Volume Eleven

Ryukyu Wa-umui

One variety: Ryukyu Wa-umui

Commonly called "mokukyōka" (wood-apricot flower), in the Ryukyus it is also known by this name. Its branches resemble those of jasmine (sobi), and it blooms in summer with trailing flowers. Its shape resembles the "kayūka" flower, with yellow petals. Its fragrance and abundance are noted; in the "Kyōtsūshi" it is called "tanshunka" (spring-seeking flower). Its summer blossoms closely resemble the yellow spring-welcoming flowers of the capital. Because its flower shape resembles the jasmine rose, it has come to share that name, though there is no fixed certainty about this.

It fears the cold of the eighth month, so it is kept indoors. According to the commentary in the "Seiji-tsū," under the entry for "jakuji," it is said that in present-day Xiamen the jasmine flower is also called "gunshitsujaku" or "jutsushiki," and also known as "yashitsumitsu." It is said to come from Persia (Oshiha-Hashi), with five-petaled flowers, of a plain color, and bearing no seed.

Tulip – "Churipa-ran" (Tulipa)

According to Jōsei, it comes from Holland.
In gardens there are many varieties differing in flower color.
Among them, one or two kinds bloom at [a certain] time.
As for the rare account, the Tang History records that in the country of Dayuan (Ta-yüan),
the state presented tulips as tribute; it is said the leaves resemble lotus leaves and the color is purple.
In the ninth month the flowers open, shaped like lotus, with several dozen petals.
A fragrant blue-green bloom extends for several dozen paces.

Also, the Kiryū (record) says it grows in the country of Daqin (the Roman Orient).

There is also a saying describing it as "flowers that do not fully open."

(Left page)

Honzō Zufu, Volume 21

Tulip (continued)

Udagawa Yōan [notes that] the "tulip" is cultivated in gardens of Holland and France;
the "tulip" is known by six different national names.
In Dutch it is called "tulp."
Its stem is round, with a soft pith inside, and grows to about a foot in height. The root sends up two or three leaves.
The leaves are broad, smooth, moist, and patterned with faint markings like brocade. At the tip of the stem
there are six large petals; the flower's shape is uniform, with three [per stem].
After flowering, the stem bears fruit; inside there are three chambers. Within the chambers
along the ridges, the seeds are red, purple, yellow, white, or other mixed colors.
The seeds are red, round, and flattened; the root is bulb-shaped and is yellow or sometimes black in color.

It flowers from the second to third month, in a form resembling crimson-blue (ai-beni).
From the fourth to fifth month, it bears fringed flowers, that is,
almond-like (an apricot scent/form).

It bears small round seeds; if planted in a pot, it will bloom with yellow flowers even indoors.

The shape of its leaves resembles that of the wolfberry (Lycium), glossy and moist. In this region,
when it ripens, it becomes fragrant.

This plant has a bitter taste; it is recorded as growing in the garden mentioned in the "Shaoxing Beiji Bencao" (a Chinese pharmacological text).
Its stems and leaves taste bitter, and it is produced there.

There is also another kind called "Ginrinka" (Silver Bell Flower), found in Shinano Province.
Its sprouting roots and fresh leaves resemble those of mixed flowers; its stem grows tall with a purplish back.
It reaches over one shaku (about 30 cm) in height, producing a spike about three sun (roughly 9 cm) long, opening small white flowers.
Later it bears round fruit shaped like that of the Kinrinka; its leaves taste
astringent and have a strong odor.
